findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify that the DC `delete_issue_link` implementation must internally absorb HTTP 404 (link already gone) and 409 (concurrent modification) as idempotent success, since `dispatch_one.py:733` has an ACLI-specific `except subprocess.CalledProcessError` handler for exactly this case that will never fire for a pycontribs-based implementation.
evidence: dispatch_one.py:733: `except subprocess.CalledProcessError: _links_applied += 1` — comment says 'delete_issue_link shells out via ACLI (raises CalledProcessError, NOT an HTTPError)'
dispatch_one.py:742: `except Exception as exc: print(f'update_one: delete_issue_link failed…')` — generic fallback logs a failure
DC transport uses pycontribs/jira exclusively (transport.py:1-30 docstring); pycontribs never raises subprocess.CalledProcessError
Plan triage row: 'IMPLEMENT: `client.delete_issue_link(id)`' — no mention of 404/409 internal swallowing
findings.finding: The DC `delete_issue_link` implementation will never raise `subprocess.CalledProcessError`, but the call site at `dispatch_one.py:733` has a specific `except subprocess.CalledProcessError: _links_applied += 1` handler that treats that exception as idempotent success (a 404/409 concurrent-removal). For DC's pycontribs implementation, a 404/409 becomes `BackendHTTPError`, which falls to the generic `except Exception` handler at line 742 — logged as a failure and NOT counted as applied. So the ACLI path silently succeeds on concurrent-removal; the DC path logs a spurious error. The plan specifies 'IMPLEMENT: `client.delete_issue_link(id)`' without noting that the DC implementation must internally absorb 404/409 to preserve the idempotent-success semantics.
findings.location: Triage table, `delete_issue_link` row; `dispatch_one.py:731-747`
scenarios: A DC link is already deleted (concurrent removal or retry). DC transport's pycontribs call raises BackendHTTPError(404). The generic except handler logs 'delete_issue_link failed', the link is NOT counted as applied, and the differ re-emits the REMOVE on the next pass — perpetual churn logged as failures.
findings.suggested_fix: Add to the triage row: 'The DC implementation must catch `BackendHTTPError` with `.code in (404, 409)` and return silently, mirroring the idempotent-success semantics the Cloud ACLI path achieves via `CalledProcessError`.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the return-value contract for DC `validate_assignee_exists` on success: it must return the matched `name` (DC username string), not an accountId, since `outbound_assignee.py:109` uses `(acct or None, True, False)` and `is_account_id=False` already signals the value is a username — omitting this leaves the implementer free to return `None` and silently unassign every DC ticket.
evidence: outbound_assignee.py:108-109: `acct = client.validate_assignee_exists(assignee, issue_key=jira_key); return (acct or None, True, False)`
Cloud's `validate_assignee_exists` (acli.py:541-630) returns an `accountId` string on success — a DC implementation should return a `name` (username)
backend.py backend_support.py: DC identities are keyed on username (`name`), not accountId
Plan triage row: 'IMPLEMENT — implement via `client.search_users(...)`, raising the existing `AssigneeNotFoundError` on a definitive miss' — no return-value specification on success
findings.finding: `validate_assignee_exists` return-value contract is left unspecified for DC. Cloud's implementation returns an `accountId` string. DC has no `accountId` concept. The call site at `outbound_assignee.py:108-109` uses `(acct or None, True, False)` — where `is_account_id=False` signals 'not an accountId', so the value will be used as a username. The plan specifies the error path (raise `AssigneeNotFoundError` on miss) and the implementation hint (`client.search_users(...)`), but says nothing about what to RETURN on a successful match. Returning `None` on success silently downgrades every DC assignee resolution to the non-authoritative string-match fallback — the exact failure mode `validate_assignee_exists` exists to prevent.
findings.location: Triage table, `validate_assignee_exists` row; `outbound_assignee.py:107-109`
scenarios: DC implementation calls `client.search_users(user=assignee)`, finds the user, but returns `None` (or omits an explicit return). Call site gets `(None, True, False)` — authoritative miss — and unassigns the ticket on every pass.
findings.suggested_fix: Add to the triage row: 'On a definitive match, return the user's `name` attribute (DC username) — the call site at outbound_assignee.py:109 uses this as `(acct or None, True, False)` with `is_account_id=False`, so a username return is correct and an accountId return or None return both produce wrong behavior.'

findings.finding: The plan prescribes `client.add_issue_property(issue, key, data)` as the implementation vehicle for `set_entity_property`, claiming it is 'VERIFIED PRESENT at RUNTIME in jira 3.10.5'. The plan's own explanation (it is wrapped by `@translate_resource_args`, so static lookup fails) is correct methodology, but the plan provides NO fallback strategy if the method is absent in the installed version: it neither specifies direct-REST as the alternative (which is exactly what the Cloud adapter does via `_direct_rest_put_raw`) nor pins the jira version in requirements. findings.finding: The plan mandates that failures in newly-implemented transport methods are OBSERVABLE (AC: 'logged at WARNING+ naming the member and the remote id, or recorded as a bridge alert') but neither the Approach nor the Scope specifies HOW this observability is implemented. Seven of the twelve have call sites that swallow Exception at every invocation; after transport methods are added, those failures become silent without a transport-level or wrapper-level logging mechanism. The plan names this as a requirement but leaves the mechanism open, meaning an implementer following the plan could satisfy the presence tests while still shipping the 'silent degradation' defect class the story exists to fix.
findings.location: Approach step 1 / Scope (transport.py) / AC 'a failure in ANY newly-implemented transport method is OBSERVABLE'
findings.suggested_fix: In the Approach (after step 1), add: 'Each implemented method logs at WARNING on failure — naming the method and the remote_id — before the error propagates. The simplest mechanism: extend `_with_connection_retry` to accept an optional `method_name` tag, and pass it from each new method so every failure emits `[jira-dc] <method_name> failed for <remote_id>: <exc>`. This satisfies the AC without per-method boilerplate.' Add `transport.py` to the Scope's patch description for this observability work.

findings.finding: The AC contains an observability requirement ('a failure in ANY newly-implemented transport member is OBSERVABLE — logged at WARNING+ naming the member and the remote id, or recorded as a bridge alert') but the Approach and Scope contain no corresponding deliverable: no Approach step describes adding logging, no Scope entry lists a logging file or calls out where WARNING+ instrumentation is added. This AC is orphaned — there is no described work for the implementer to execute.
findings.location: AC — 'a failure in ANY newly-implemented transport member is OBSERVABLE'; Approach (all four steps); Scope (all bullets)

findings.finding: The observability AC ('a failure in ANY newly-implemented transport member is OBSERVABLE — logged at WARNING+ naming the member and the remote id') is required but the Scope names no file or layer responsible for adding that logging. The seven swallowed members have their exceptions caught at CORE call sites (dispatch_apply_phases.py, outbound_differ.py, etc.), not at transport call sites — so transport-level try/catch/log would suppress the exception before the core sees it (changing the error contract), while adding logging to the core catch blocks is J10's territory. Without specifying which layer adds the logging, an implementer either silently omits it or adds it at the wrong level.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria — 'a failure in ANY newly-implemented transport member is OBSERVABLE'; Scope section (no corresponding file listed)
findings.suggested_fix: Add a sentence to the Scope entry for transport.py specifying that each new transport method should log at WARNING before re-raising (not catch-and-suppress), e.g. `logger.warning('DC transport: %s failed for %s: %s', 'set_entity_property', issue_key, exc); raise` — preserving propagation semantics while satisfying the observability AC at the only layer J9 controls.

findings.finding: The plan's observability AC states: 'a failure in ANY newly-implemented transport member is OBSERVABLE — logged at WARNING+ naming the member and the remote id, or recorded as a bridge alert'. But the plan simultaneously states 'SEVEN of the twelve have call sites that swallow `Exception` at EVERY invocation, and they stay swallowed after implementation'. The CORE call sites that swallow (`dispatch_one.py`, `outbound_comments.py`, `apply_inbound_records.py`, etc.) are NOT in the plan's Scope. The transport methods themselves raise on failure — they don't log. So to satisfy the observability AC without editing core, the transport methods must LOG before raising. But that is architecturally wrong (transports raise, callers log). No scope entry covers the core call-site logging changes that would be needed if the transport is to remain a pure raise-on-error layer. The AC is therefore either (a) unachievable within the stated scope, or (b) requires the transport to log-and-raise, which the plan does not specify.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria — 'a failure in ANY newly-implemented transport member is OBSERVABLE'; Scope section

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify in AC 1 that the 'recorded verdict' for IMPLEMENT members is the implemented method itself, for NOT-APPLICABLE members is a `raise NotImplementedError("DC limitation: ...")` in transport.py, and for UNREACHABLE-BY-CALL-SITE members is a code comment in transport.py naming the upstream decision — and that a grep/test for `NotImplementedError` in transport.py is the proving command for that category.
evidence: Plan lists three verdict forms: 'implemented, NotImplementedError naming the DC limitation, or documented as unreachable-by-call-site with the upstream decision named'
'never simply absent' is stated as the requirement but 'unreachable-by-call-site' verdict has no specified artifact location (code comment? docstring in transport.py? ticket note?)
No proving command distinguishes a passing 'recorded verdict' from a missing one
findings.finding: AC 1 ('ALL TWELVE absent members carry a RECORDED VERDICT — implemented, NotImplementedError naming the DC limitation, or documented as unreachable-by-call-site') names three verdict categories but does not specify what artifact constitutes a 'recorded verdict' that can be evaluated in CI or by a reviewing agent. The three categories involve code (raising NotImplementedError), documentation (a comment or docstring), or possibly a ticket annotation — none of these are distinguished, so an executor cannot determine whether a docstring in transport.py, a comment in the plan, or a test asserting NotImplementedError is raised satisfies the criterion.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria — first bullet ('ALL TWELVE absent members carry a RECORDED VERDICT')
scenarios: An executor concludes that the triage table in the plan itself IS the 'recorded verdict' and ships no in-code documentation for UNREACHABLE-BY-CALL-SITE members
A reviewer cannot determine whether the AC passes without manually cross-referencing the plan triage table against the transport source — no machine-checkable criterion exists
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the AC wording with: 'ALL TWELVE absent members carry an IN-CODE verdict in transport.py: IMPLEMENT → the method body; NOT-APPLICABLE → `raise NotImplementedError("<DC limitation>")` with a docstring; UNREACHABLE-BY-CALL-SITE → a comment naming the upstream decision. Proving command: `grep -n NotImplementedError src/.../jira_datacenter/transport.py` lists each explicitly declined member; unit tests assert the implemented set is callable and the declined set raises.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify that new transport member log messages must include only the member name and the remote_id (e.g. `logger.warning('set_entity_property on %s failed', remote_id)`) and must NOT chain or format the caught exception as part of the message, to prevent JIRAError text (which can include request URLs or auth header fragments) from entering logs on the boundary-crossing auth path.
evidence: Plan (Approach §4): 'have each newly-implemented member log at WARNING naming the MEMBER and the REMOTE ID before the error propagates' — silent on whether exc text is included.

transport.py:145-163 (_as_backend_http_error): stores str(exc) as the reason field of BackendHTTPError; if implementations log `exc` or `str(exc)`, JIRAError bodies (which can include the request URL with auth path) enter the log.
transport.py:92: PAT travels as Bearer token in Authorization header on every request; pycontribs/jira JIRAError in some versions echoes the request URL in __str__.

The plan's own note (Approach §4): 'J10 has already translated it to BackendHTTPError by then' — but the logging happens at the transport layer, where the BackendHTTPError's reason string already contains str(JIRAError).
Single-tenant internal deployment reduces blast radius to advisory level; finding is not blocking.
findings.finding: The plan's logging prescription for newly-implemented transport members does not bound what may appear in log messages, leaving open the risk that caught exception text (JIRAError.__str__, which can embed the full request URL and, in some pycontribs versions, Authorization header fragments) is logged at WARNING on a boundary-crossing path that carries a PAT.
findings.location: Approach step 4 / Scope — transport.py logging addition / AC: 'a failure in ANY newly-implemented transport member is OBSERVABLE — logged at WARNING+ naming the member and the remote id'
scenarios: A new transport method (e.g. set_entity_property) catches BackendHTTPError and logs `logger.warning('set_entity_property %s failed: %s', remote_id, exc)`. The exc.reason string contains the JIRAError text, which in some pycontribs versions includes the full Authorization: Bearer <token> header echoed from the request context, writing the PAT into the application log.
